title: At the office and at work
goal: Survive in a Malaysian workplace — words for the office, emails, meetings, leave and pay, most of them quite different from Indonesian office vocabulary.
bekal: naming departments, sections and office matters with Malaysian terms
writing and answering a simple work email
applying for leave, reporting sick and setting up appointments

dialogs.title: Dialogue — First day of an internship
dialogs.intro: Sarah is doing an internship at a tech company in Cyberjaya. Puan Norliza, her supervisor, explains her first day.

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Selamat datang, Sarah. Awak akan bekerja di bahagian pembangunan.
lines.id: Welcome, Sarah. You'll be working in the development department.
lines.literal: welcome, Sarah. you will work in section development.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Terima kasih, puan. Waktu bekerja pukul berapa?
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. What are the working hours?
lines.literal: thank you, madam. time working hour how-many?

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Lapan setengah pagi sampai lima setengah petang. Rehat pukul satu.
lines.id: Eight thirty in the morning to five thirty in the afternoon. Lunch break is at one.
lines.literal: eight half morning until five half afternoon. rest hour one.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Okay. Is there a meeting today?

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Ada, pukul sepuluh di bilik mesyuarat tingkat tiga. Bawa buku nota.
lines.id: Yes, at ten in the meeting room on the third floor. Bring a notebook.
lines.literal: have, hour ten in room meeting floor three. bring book note.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: Do I have to give a presentation?

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Belum. Minggu depan baru. Hari ni dengar je dulu.
lines.id: Not yet. Only next week. Today, just listen first.
lines.literal: not-yet. week front only. day this listen just first.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Puan, kalau saya sakit, macam mana nak maklumkan?
lines.id: Ma'am, if I'm sick, how do I let you know?
lines.literal: madam, if I sick, how want inform?

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Hantar mesej kat saya sebelum pukul sembilan, lepas tu bawa sijil sakit.
lines.id: Send me a message before nine, then bring a medical certificate.
lines.literal: send message to me before hour nine, after that bring certificate sick.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Faham. Kalau nak ambil cuti pula?
lines.id: Got it. And if I want to take leave?
lines.literal: understand. if want take leave instead?

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Mohon dalam sistem, sekurang-kurangnya tiga hari awal.
lines.id: Apply in the system, at least three days in advance.
lines.literal: apply in system, at-least three day early.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Baiklah, puan. Terima kasih atas penerangan.
lines.id: All right, ma'am. Thank you for the explanation.
lines.literal: all-right, madam. thank you for explanation.

lines.speaker: Pn. Norliza:
lines.text: Sama-sama. Kalau ada apa-apa, jangan segan tanya.
lines.id: You're welcome. If there's anything, don't be shy to ask.
lines.literal: same-same. if have anything, don't shy ask.

notes: **Pejabat** = office. It's the word you'll meet most at work: *pejabat pos* = post office, *pejabat kerajaan* = government office, *jam pejabat* = office hours. (Careful if you know Indonesian: there *pejabat* means a high-ranking official.)

**Mesyuarat** = meeting. It comes from Arabic, like *musyawarah* (deliberation), but in Malaysia it's simply the everyday word for a work meeting. *Bilik mesyuarat* = meeting room, *minit mesyuarat* = meeting minutes.
**Pembentangan** = presentation. From *bentang* (to spread out, lay out). *Membentangkan kertas kerja* = to present a paper.

**Maklumkan** = to inform, let someone know. The word family is large and very productive in Malaysia: *maklumat* (information ⚠️), *dimaklumkan* (be informed), *makluman* (notice). Notice boards say *MAKLUMAN* or *PERHATIAN*.

**Sijil** = certificate. *Sijil sakit* = medical certificate (often just "MC"), *sijil kelahiran* = birth certificate, *sijil SPM* = the school-leaving certificate. *Sijil* turns up in every official matter.

grammars.title: Office vocabulary
body: Here Malay differs most from Indonesian: Indonesian took many office words from Dutch, while Malay coined its own or borrowed from English. Learn these as Malaysian terms.
after: ⚠️ Keep **jabatan**, **pejabat** and **jawatan** apart. *Jabatan* = department, government agency (*Jabatan Imigresen* = Immigration Department); *pejabat* = office, the place; *jawatan* = post, position (*jawatan kosong* = vacancy). Three similar-sounding words with crossing meanings.
⚠️ **Elaun** (from *allowance*) = allowance. *Elaun perjalanan* = travel allowance, *elaun makan* = meal allowance.

blocks.text: Formal Malaysian emails keep their distance — the greeting and sign-off are fixed formulas, and there are no conversational particles at all. The structure:

head: Part
Malay
English
rows: Dear Mr Ahmad, / Dear Mrs Norliza,
With reference to the above matter,

blocks.text: **Sekian, terima kasih.** ("That is all, thank you") is the standard closing in almost every formal Malaysian letter and email — so standard that leaving it out feels incomplete.

blocks.title: A short sample email
items: **Merujuk perkara di atas, saya ingin memohon cuti tahunan pada 20 hingga 22 Mac 2026 atas urusan keluarga.**
**Bersama-sama ini disertakan borang permohonan yang telah dilengkapkan. Mohon pertimbangan dan kelulusan puan.**

blocks.text: **Kelulusan** means **approval** as well as passing an exam. *Mohon kelulusan* = requesting approval. *Lulus* does mean pass (an exam), so context decides. This is one of the most frequent traps at work.

Unofficial messages to colleagues — work WhatsApp, for example — are much more relaxed and can use short forms: *Boleh tolong semak fail ni tak?* (Could you check this file?), *Saya lambat sikit, jem teruk.* (I'll be a bit late, traffic's terrible.), *Dah hantar kat email tadi.* (Already sent it by email.)

head: Malay
English
rows: Saya nak ambil cuti hari Jumaat.
I'd like to take Friday off.
Boleh saya keluar awal hari ni?
That file is in the system.
Could you check it for a moment?
The meeting has been postponed to tomorrow.
I need to print this document.
Salary comes in at the end of the month.

blocks.text: **Ditangguhkan** = postponed. *Tangguh* in Malay means delay, postponement. (In Indonesian *tangguh* means tough, resilient — a subtle trap in work emails.)
**Fail** = file. **Cetak** = print. **Sihat** = healthy — note the *i*. Malay spelling keeps the Arabic-based form in some words: *sihat*, *faham*, *khabar*, *nasihat*, *Isnin*.

blocks.title: Malaysian public holidays you should know
items: **Hari Raya Aidilfitri** — Eid al-Fitr (two public holidays).
**Tahun Baru Cina** — Chinese New Year (two days).
⚠️ Public holidays vary from state to state. A holiday in Selangor isn't necessarily a holiday in Johor. Always check the calendar of the state you work in.
